title: Identity and Access (Advanced)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Choose between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities, and explain how code gets tokens without secrets.
- Replace a client secret with workload identity federation for GitHub Actions, and explain app registrations versus service principals.
- Design Conditional Access policies from conditions, grant controls and session controls, and roll them out safely.
- Plan just-in-time administration with Privileged Identity Management, access reviews and emergency-access accounts.
- Write a least-privilege custom role with actions, data actions and assignable scopes.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Six months have passed. The storefront runs in Azure, and before the 12.12 shopping festival Ibu Sari has asked an external auditor to look at who can do what. The report lands on your desk with four findings:

1. The deployment pipeline signs in with a client secret stored in GitHub. It expired last month and broke a release at 23:00 — and it also appears in an old build log.
2. Five people hold permanent Owner on the production subscription. Two of them haven't used it this year.
3. Rizky's contract ended in March, but his guest account is still a member of grp-nusa-contractors.
4. The night-shift operator only ever restarts VMs, yet holds Contributor on the whole production resource group.

None of these breaks a rule from Lunch 05. All of them are standing risks: secrets that live for months, privileges nobody uses, access nobody reviews.

Today's question: How do you remove standing secrets and standing privilege without slowing the team down?

Reading

1. Workload identities: app registrations, service principals and managed identities

People aren't the only ones who sign in. Pipelines, web apps, functions and scripts need identities too; Microsoft Entra calls them workload identities.

An app registration — the application object — is the global definition of an application in its home tenant: its name, the permissions it requests, its redirect URIs and its credentials. A service principal is the application's local representative in one particular tenant, and it's what you grant roles to. A multi-tenant SaaS application has one app registration and a service principal in every customer tenant; in the portal, service principals appear under Enterprise applications. When you register an app in the portal, its service principal in your tenant is created for you; with the Azure CLI you create it yourself (az ad sp create).

A service principal proves its identity with a credential, and you have three choices:

Credential | How it works | Lifetime | Main risk
Client secret | A generated string, used like a password | You choose an expiry | Leaks into code, logs and screenshots; rotation is manual
Certificate | Proof that you hold a private key | The certificate's validity period | Safer than a secret, but you still store, protect and renew it
Federated credential | Trust in tokens issued by another identity provider | Nothing long-lived is stored | A carelessly broad subject could trust the wrong workload

Which one should a workload use? A simple rule of thumb:

- It runs in Azure (a VM, App Service, Functions, Container Apps, AKS): a managed identity — there's nothing to store at all.
- It runs outside Azure on a platform that issues OIDC tokens (GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, another cloud): workload identity federation, described in the next section.
- It runs on your own servers: connect them to Azure Arc, whose agent gives each server a managed identity, or fall back to a certificate.
- Client secrets: only when nothing else works — with a short expiry, kept in Key Vault and rotated by automation.

Managed identities, which you met in Lunch 15, are service principals whose credentials Azure creates, rotates and never shows to anyone. Code running on a VM, App Service, Azure Functions, Container Apps or AKS simply asks its local endpoint for a token. The two kinds differ in lifecycle:

| System-assigned | User-assigned
Created | As part of one resource (switch it on) | As a standalone Azure resource
Lifecycle | Deleted together with that resource | Independent; you delete it yourself
Sharing | One resource only | Can be attached to many resources
Good for | One VM or app with its own permissions | Scale sets and slots, compute that's rebuilt often, permissions granted before the workload exists

Microsoft's documentation recommends user-assigned identities, and the lifecycle explains why: the permissions survive when the compute is rebuilt — handy when Bicep (Lunch 20) recreates resources. One caveat: back-end services cache managed-identity tokens for a long time, so a change to an identity's group memberships or roles can take hours rather than minutes to apply.

In code, the Azure Identity libraries offer DefaultAzureCredential, which tries a chain of sources in order: environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, then developer sign-ins such as Visual Studio Code, the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and the Azure Developer CLI. The same line of code signs in as Dewi on her laptop and as the managed identity in Azure. That's convenient, but in production pin it to the credential you expect, such as ManagedIdentityCredential, so an unexpected environment variable can't change who your app signs in as.

There's one more reason to use workload identities: Azure's mandatory MFA applies to user accounts in the portal, CLI, PowerShell and infrastructure-as-code tools, but not to managed identities or service principals. Automation that still runs under a person's account will meet an MFA prompt it cannot answer.

2. Workload identity federation: deployments without secrets

Managed identities exist only inside Azure. Dewi's pipeline runs in GitHub Actions, outside Azure, which is why it used a client secret. Workload identity federation removes that secret by trusting tokens from another identity provider.

GitHub runs an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider. Every workflow job can ask it for a short-lived, signed token that describes exactly who is asking: which repository, which branch or environment, which workflow. You tell Microsoft Entra ID which tokens to accept with a federated identity credential on the app registration (or on a user-assigned managed identity):

- Issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com.
- Subject: which workload, in a format that depends on what triggered the job (see the table below).
- Audience: api://AzureADTokenExchange, the recommended value and the default of the azure/login action.

What runs the job | Subject in GitHub's token | Use it for
A push or manual run on a branch | repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:ref:refs/heads/main | Deployments from one trusted branch
A job that uses an environment | repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:environment:production | Production, guarded by required reviewers
A pull request | repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:pull_request | Read-only checks such as a what-if — never production
A tag | repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:ref:refs/tags/v1.4 | Release pipelines

In the workflow, two details matter: permissions: id-token: write, without which the job can't request a token, and the azure/login action, which receives only client-id, tenant-id and subscription-id. None of those values are secrets, although many teams store them as GitHub secrets to keep them out of logs.

The matching is strict, and that's the point. Issuer, subject and audience must match exactly, and wildcards aren't supported (a flexible federated credential with claim-matching expressions is in preview). An app registration or user-assigned managed identity can hold up to 20 federated credentials, so one per branch or environment is normal. A wrong subject produces no error when you create the credential; the token exchange simply fails later with an AADSTS700213 "no matching federated identity record" message.

Design the trust with least privilege in mind. Give each environment its own identity — one for development with Contributor on the development resource group, another for production with a narrowly scoped role — so a mistake in a test workflow can't reach production. Tie the production identity to a GitHub environment with required reviewers, so a person approves the job before it can even ask for a token. Never give a pull-request subject a role that can change anything. The client ID and tenant ID only name the app; the federated credential decides which workloads may become it.

Important: GitHub repositories created after July 15, 2026 use an immutable subject format that adds the numeric owner and repository IDs, such as repo:nusantara-retail@123456/storefront@456789:ref:refs/heads/main. Older repositories keep the classic format unless their owner opts in. Check which format your repository uses before you create the credential; a failed sign-in shows the subject GitHub actually sent.

Kubernetes works the same way. An AKS cluster with its OIDC issuer enabled signs tokens for service accounts, with subjects like system:serviceaccount:storefront:orders-api, and Microsoft Entra Workload ID exchanges them for Azure tokens (Lunch 29).

3. Conditional Access in depth

Lunch 05 introduced Conditional Access as if-then logic. A real policy has three parts.

Assignments: who and what. Users — include groups such as all users or contractors, and always exclude your emergency-access accounts. (Workload identities can be targeted too, with a separate Workload ID licence.) Target resources — cloud apps such as Azure management or Microsoft 365, user actions such as registering security information, or an authentication context, a label that an app or PIM can demand at a sensitive moment.

Conditions: when. Sign-in risk and user risk (from Microsoft Entra ID Protection, a P2 feature), device platforms, locations (named IP ranges and countries), client apps such as legacy authentication, and device filters.

Access controls: then what. Grant controls block access, or grant it while requiring one or all of: MFA, an authentication strength (for example phishing-resistant methods only), a device marked compliant by Intune, a Microsoft Entra hybrid-joined device, an approved client app, an app protection policy, a password change, or acceptance of terms of use. Session controls shape what happens after sign-in: sign-in frequency, persistent browser sessions, and real-time session monitoring through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps.

Nusantara Retail policy | Users | Target | Condition | Control
MFA for everyone | All users, except emergency accounts | All resources | — | Require MFA
Block legacy authentication | All users | All resources | Client apps: legacy clients | Block
Phishing-resistant admins | Administrator roles | All resources | — | Authentication strength: phishing-resistant
Contractors from unmanaged devices | grp-nusa-contractors | Azure management | Device isn't compliant | Require MFA; sign-in frequency 8 hours
Risky sign-ins (P2) | All users | All resources | Sign-in risk: high | Block

Policies combine. Every policy whose assignments match a sign-in applies at once: if any of them blocks, access is blocked; otherwise every grant requirement of every matching policy must be met. That's why a handful of broad, clearly named policies beats dozens of overlapping ones. And keep the division of labour from Lunch 05 in mind: Conditional Access decides how someone obtains a token, while Azure RBAC still decides what that token may do.

Roll policies out safely. Report-only mode evaluates a policy and logs what would have happened without enforcing anything, and the What If tool simulates a sign-in against all your policies. Microsoft also offers Microsoft-managed policies that keep the protections of security defaults once you switch them off. Conditional Access needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 (risk conditions need P2), and you switch security defaults off when your own policies replace them.

Warning: The classic Conditional Access accident is a policy nobody can satisfy — for example, requiring a compliant device before any device is enrolled — which locks out every administrator. Always exclude two emergency-access accounts, start in report-only mode, read the sign-in logs for a few days, and only then switch the policy on.

4. Privileged Identity Management, access reviews and emergency access

The auditor's second finding was permanent Owner. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) replaces standing privilege with just-in-time access. Instead of an active role assignment, Pak Budi receives an eligible one: he holds no permissions until he activates the role, for a duration within a maximum the administrator sets (between 1 and 24 hours). Activation can require MFA or a Conditional Access authentication context, a business justification, a ticket number, and approval by designated approvers. PIM notifies people when roles are activated, records every activation for audits, and can make even eligible assignments time-bound, with start and end dates.

PIM covers Microsoft Entra roles (Global Administrator should be eligible, not active, for almost everyone), Azure resource roles at any scope, and PIM for Groups, which makes membership of a privileged group just-in-time. The users involved need Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance licences.

A few habits make PIM work in practice. Role settings belong to one role on one resource and aren't inherited — settings on the subscription don't flow down to its resource groups — so configure every scope you use. Keep activation windows short, and require approval for the most powerful roles; Microsoft recommends at least two approvers, so one person's holiday can't block an incident. Read PIM's alerts, which flag problems such as roles assigned outside PIM. And when the work is done early, users can deactivate a role themselves instead of waiting for it to expire.

Access reviews answer the third finding. On a schedule, group owners, managers or the users themselves confirm whether guests, group members or role holders still need their access, and the results can be applied automatically, removing anyone nobody vouched for. A quarterly review of grp-nusa-contractors would have removed Rizky in April. Access reviews are part of Microsoft Entra ID Governance; some capabilities also work with P2.

Emergency-access accounts, also called break-glass accounts, are the safety net under all of this. Keep at least two cloud-only accounts on the .onmicrosoft.com domain, permanently active as Global Administrator. Protect them with a phishing-resistant method such as a passkey on a FIDO2 security key, because mandatory MFA applies to them too. Exclude them from Conditional Access policies that block or restrict sign-in, store their credentials securely, alert on every sign-in, and test them at least every 90 days.

5. Custom roles and external identities

The fourth finding — Contributor for an operator who only restarts VMs — is the textbook case for an Azure custom role, a role definition you write as JSON:

Property | Meaning | "Nusantara VM Operator"
Actions | Management operations the role allows | Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read, …/start/action, …/restart/action, …/deallocate/action
NotActions | Operations subtracted from Actions | None needed: no wildcards were used
DataActions | Operations on data inside resources | None: operators don't read disks or blobs
NotDataActions | Data operations subtracted from DataActions | None
AssignableScopes | Where the role may be assigned | The production resource group only

Some rules worth knowing. Find operation names with az provider operation show --namespace Microsoft.Compute, or start from a similar built-in role. Prefer explicit actions to wildcards, because Microsoft.Compute/* silently includes operations Microsoft adds later. A tenant can hold up to 5,000 custom roles; assignable scopes can't be the root scope (/) and can include at most one management group; roles with DataActions can't be assigned at management-group scope; and you must remove every assignment of a custom role before you can delete it. Above all, NotActions isn't a deny. It only trims this role; if another role grants the same action, the user still has it. Only deny assignments block.

Rizky was a B2B collaboration guest — a user object in your directory, authenticated by his own organisation. Cross-tenant access settings decide which organisations may collaborate with you and whether you trust their MFA and device claims, so guests aren't prompted twice. Entitlement management bundles groups, apps and sites into access packages that partners request, with approvals and automatic expiry. For shoppers, Microsoft Entra External ID in an external tenant is the customer-identity option: self-service sign-up, social accounts such as Google or Facebook, and your own branding, separate from your workforce directory. (Azure AD B2C isn't sold to new customers any more.)

6. Putting it together at Nusantara Retail

Licensing shapes the plan, so check it first:

Capability | Licence
Users, groups, SSO, security defaults, B2B guests | Microsoft Entra ID Free
Managed identities, app registrations, workload identity federation, Azure custom roles | Included with Entra ID and your Azure subscription
Conditional Access, dynamic groups | Microsoft Entra ID P1
Risk-based Conditional Access (ID Protection), PIM | Microsoft Entra ID P2 (PIM also with ID Governance)
Access reviews, entitlement management with all features | Microsoft Entra ID Governance (some features with P2)

With P2 for the administrators and P1 for everyone else, your answer to the auditor fits on one page:

1. Pipeline: the GitHub workflow signs in through a federated credential for the main branch and another for the production environment. The client secret is deleted, and the service principal holds Contributor on rg-storefront only.
2. Owners: two administrators become eligible for Owner through PIM, with activation of at most four hours, MFA, a justification and Ibu Sari's approval. Everyone else drops to Reader.
3. Guests: a quarterly access review covers grp-nusa-contractors, and future contractors request an access package that expires after 90 days.
4. Night shift: the operator gets the custom Nusantara VM Operator role on the production resource group, nothing more.
5. Safety net: the Conditional Access policies above run in report-only for a week before going live, and two emergency-access accounts with FIDO2 keys sit in the office safe.

The reporting app gets a user-assigned managed identity with Storage Blob Data Reader, so not a single secret remains in Nusantara Retail's code or pipelines.

Pause and think: the pipeline's federated credential trusts repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:ref:refs/heads/main. Someone opens a pull request whose changed workflow tries to deploy to production. Does that run get an Azure token? What subject would its GitHub token carry?

You'll meet these ideas again at scale: workload identity on AKS in Lunch 29, and RBAC, PIM and custom roles across management groups in Lunch 31.

Field notes from Stefanus

Ask what a stolen laptop could do before breakfast. I ask that question in every access review, about each person and each pipeline. For people, the honest answer should be "nothing without a second factor, and nothing in production without a PIM activation that someone gets notified about". For pipelines: "nothing, because no pipeline secret exists — not in GitHub, not in a script, not on that laptop". My habit is one short list of every credential that can sign in without a human, with an owner and an expiry date on each line. Lines without an owner are the first I replace with a managed identity or a federated credential. And I name each federated credential after the exact branch or environment it trusts, so the next reviewer sees the boundary without decoding a subject string.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Authenticate to Azure from GitHub Actions by OpenID Connect (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/github/connect-from-azure-openid-connect) — the official walkthrough for azure/login with OIDC.
- Microsoft Learn: Configure an app to trust an external identity provider (https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation-create-trust) — every field of a federated credential, with GitHub and Kubernetes examples.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management? (https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure) — eligible versus active assignments and the activation workflow.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure custom roles (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/role-based-access-control/custom-roles) — role properties, limits and who can create them.

quiz.q: Automation replaces every instance of a VM scale set each week, and all instances must read the same Key Vault. Do you use a system-assigned or a user-assigned managed identity?
quiz.a: A user-assigned managed identity, attached to the scale set, with the Key Vault role assigned once. Why: its lifecycle is independent of the instances and one identity can be shared, so access survives every rebuild.

quiz.q: A workflow job declares environment: production and fails with AADSTS700213, although the app has a federated credential with the subject repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:ref:refs/heads/main. What's wrong?
quiz.a: Jobs that reference an environment get the subject repo:nusantara-retail/storefront:environment:production, which doesn't match. Add a federated credential with exactly that subject. Why: issuer, subject and audience must match exactly; there are no wildcards.

quiz.q: You add Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete to the NotActions of a custom role assigned to Dewi, yet she can still delete VMs. Why?
quiz.a: Another role assignment — for example Contributor through one of her groups — grants delete, and Azure RBAC adds roles together. Why: NotActions only trims the role it's written in; only a deny assignment blocks an action that another role allows.

quiz.q: Ibu Sari wants administrators to hold Owner only when they need it, with her approval and an audit trail. Which feature and which licence?
quiz.a: Privileged Identity Management: eligible Owner assignments whose activation requires MFA, a justification and approval, for a limited number of hours. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance. Why: PIM replaces standing privilege with just-in-time, logged activations.

quiz.q: You're about to turn on a Conditional Access policy requiring compliant devices for all users. Which two precautions come first?
quiz.a: Exclude the emergency-access accounts, and run the policy in report-only mode (checking sign-in logs or the What If tool) before enforcing it. Why: a policy nobody can satisfy can lock every administrator out of the tenant.

takeaways: Prefer managed identities inside Azure — user-assigned when compute is shared or rebuilt — and pin DefaultAzureCredential to a specific credential in production.
Workload identity federation removes stored secrets: Microsoft Entra ID trusts GitHub or Kubernetes tokens whose issuer, subject and audience match exactly.
A Conditional Access policy combines assignments, conditions and grant or session controls; roll it out in report-only and never without emergency-access exclusions.
PIM turns standing admin rights into eligible, time-limited, approved activations; access reviews and two tested break-glass accounts complete the picture.
Custom roles grant exactly the operations a job needs at a scope you choose; NotActions only subtracts, and only deny assignments block.

lab.title: Passwordless pipelines and least privilege
lab.text:
Caution: Use your own tenant and subscription. This lab creates a custom role, a group and an app registration. You need Owner on the subscription (to create custom roles and role assignments) and the right to create groups and app registrations in Microsoft Entra ID. The tenant that came with your personal free account gives you all of that; a company or school tenant usually doesn't — and isn't the place for experiments anyway.

What you'll build

The auditor's findings from the lunch, fixed in miniature. You'll write the Nusantara VM Operator custom role from a JSON file — start, restart and deallocate VMs, nothing else — and assign it to an operators group at resource-group scope. You'll give a user-assigned managed identity a data role on a storage account, so a future reporting app needs no storage key. And you'll create an app registration with no secret at all: its only credential is a federated credential that trusts GitHub Actions on one repository's main branch. If you have a GitHub repository, you'll watch a workflow sign in to Azure with OpenID Connect. Conditional Access and PIM need P1 and P2 licences, so they come as a guided portal tour.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you are Owner (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)), in a tenant you own.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install; jq is included.
- Optional, for Task 7: a GitHub account and a repository you own (it can be empty).
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/22-identity-access-advanced
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 22)

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway. The storage account costs next to nothing while it's empty, but the custom role, group and app registration live outside the resource group, so only cleanup.sh removes them.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–8 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create the resource group and note your IDs

Custom roles and role assignments are written against resource IDs, so capture the ones you'll need.

ensure_rg "$RG" 22
SUB_ID=$(az account show --query id --output tsv)
TENANT_ID=$(az account show --query tenantId --output tsv)
RG_ID=$(az group show --name "$RG" --query id --output tsv)
echo "$RG_ID"

Checkpoint: RG_ID looks like /subscriptions/…/resourceGroups/rg-lunch22-<suffix>.

Task 2 · Write the custom role

Open vm-operator-role.json. It lists exactly what a night-shift operator needs: read VMs and their status, start, restart and deallocate them, and see the resource group. There are no wildcards, no write, no delete and no data actions. AssignableScopes will hold just the lab resource group, so the role can't be used anywhere else. Fill in the placeholders and create the role:

ROLE_NAME="Nusantara VM Operator ${SUFFIX}"
sed -e "s|__SUFFIX__|${SUFFIX}|" -e "s|__SUBSCRIPTION_ID__|${SUB_ID}|" -e "s|__RESOURCE_GROUP__|${RG}|" \
  vm-operator-role.json > my-vm-operator-role.json
cat my-vm-operator-role.json
az role definition create --role-definition @my-vm-operator-role.json --query "{name:roleName, id:name}" --output table

The role's name must be unique in your tenant — that's why it ends with your suffix. Look it up at the resource-group scope, because that's the only place it can be assigned:

az role definition list --name "$ROLE_NAME" --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --query "[0].{name:roleName, type:roleType, actions:permissions[0].actions, scopes:assignableScopes}" --output json

Tip: Prefer the portal? rg-lunch22-<suffix> › Access control (IAM) › Add › Add custom role, then choose Start from JSON and upload my-vm-operator-role.json. The Permissions tab lets you search every operation by keyword — a good way to discover action names.

Checkpoint: the role shows "type": "CustomRole", six actions and one assignable scope, your resource group. If the lookup returns nothing, wait a minute: new roles take a moment to replicate.

Task 3 · Assign the custom role to an operators group

Roles go to groups. Create one for the night shift and assign the custom role by its ID (a GUID), which keeps working even if someone renames the role.

OPS_GROUP="grp-nusa-vm-operators-${SUFFIX}"
OPS_GROUP_ID=$(az ad group create --display-name "$OPS_GROUP" --mail-nickname "$OPS_GROUP" \
  --description "Lab 22: night-shift operators who start, restart and deallocate VMs" --query id --output tsv)
ROLE_GUID=$(az role definition list --name "$ROLE_NAME" --scope "$RG_ID" --query "[0].name" --output tsv)
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$OPS_GROUP_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type Group \
  --role "$ROLE_GUID" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --output none
az role assignment list --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --query "[].{principal:principalName, role:roleDefinitionName}" --output table

If you get RoleDefinitionDoesNotExist or Role … doesn't exist, the new role hasn't replicated yet: wait a minute and run the command again.

Can't create groups in your tenant? Assign the role to yourself instead, with --assignee-object-id "$(my_object_id)" --assignee-principal-type User. As Owner it adds nothing to what you can do, but you'll see the assignment, and verify.sh accepts any principal.

Checkpoint: the table shows your operators group with Nusantara VM Operator <suffix>.

Task 4 · Give a user-assigned managed identity a data role

The reporting app will read sales exports from blob storage. Instead of a storage key in its configuration, it gets an identity of its own — created as a standalone resource, so it survives when the app's compute is rebuilt.

az identity create --name id-nusa-reports --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --output none
MI_PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az identity show --name id-nusa-reports --resource-group "$RG" --query principalId --output tsv)

ST_NAME="stnusareports${SUFFIX}"
az storage account create --name "$ST_NAME" --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false --output none
ST_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$ST_NAME" --resource-group "$RG" --query id --output tsv)

az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "$ST_ID" \
  --output none
az role assignment list --assignee-object-id "$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID" --all \
  --query "[].{role:roleDefinitionName, scope:scope}" --output table

The identity has two IDs: the principal ID (its service principal, which receives roles) and the client ID, which code passes to ManagedIdentityCredential to choose this identity. Storage Blob Data Reader is a data role: it reads blobs, but it can't change the account or list its keys.

Checkpoint: exactly one row — Storage Blob Data Reader, scoped to your storage account.

Task 5 · Create an app registration with no secret

The pipeline needs an identity too. Create the app registration and its service principal, and give the service principal Reader on the resource group — enough for the sample workflow to list resources.

APP_NAME="app-nusa-github-deploy-${SUFFIX}"
APP_ID=$(az ad app create --display-name "$APP_NAME" --query appId --output tsv)
az ad sp create --id "$APP_ID" --output none
SP_ID=$(az ad sp show --id "$APP_ID" --query id --output tsv)
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$SP_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Reader" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --output none
az ad app credential list --id "$APP_ID" --output table

APP_ID is the application (client) ID that GitHub will use. The last command lists the app's client secrets — and prints nothing, because there are none. Keep it that way.

Warning: az ad app create doesn't stop you from creating a second app with the same display name. If you run this task twice, look the app up first: az ad app list --display-name "$APP_NAME" --query "[].appId" --output tsv.

Checkpoint: az ad sp show --id "$APP_ID" --query "{name:displayName, type:servicePrincipalType}" --output table shows your app as type Application, and the credential list is empty.

Task 6 · Add a federated credential for GitHub Actions

Decide which repository Azure should trust. GITHUB_REPO is the part of the subject between repo: and :ref::

GITHUB_REPO="<your-github-user>/<your-repo>"          # a repository you own
# No GitHub account? Use a name only you know, so nothing can ever match it:
# GITHUB_REPO="nusa-lab-${SUFFIX}/storefront"

Important: GitHub repositories created after July 15, 2026 use an immutable subject that adds numeric IDs, for example repo:octo-learner@1234567/storefront@891011:ref:refs/heads/main. Older repositories keep the classic repo:owner/repo form unless their owner opted in. For a public repository, this prints the immutable form:

curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_REPO}" | jq -r '"\(.owner.login)@\(.owner.id)/\(.name)@\(.id)"'

If your repository uses that format, set GITHUB_REPO to the printed value. Unsure? Use the classic form now; Task 7 shows you the exact subject if it doesn't match.

Now look at federated-credential.json — issuer, subject and audience — fill in the repository and create the credential:

sed "s|__GITHUB_REPO__|${GITHUB_REPO}|" federated-credential.json > my-federated-credential.json
cat my-federated-credential.json
az ad app federated-credential create --id "$APP_ID" --parameters my-federated-credential.json --output none
az ad app federated-credential list --id "$APP_ID" \
  --query "[].{name:name, issuer:issuer, subject:subject, audiences:join(',', audiences)}" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? Microsoft Entra admin center › App registrations › app-nusa-github-deploy-<suffix> › Certificates & secrets › Federated credentials › Add credential, scenario GitHub Actions deploying Azure resources. The portal builds the subject from organisation, repository and entity type (branch, environment, pull request or tag).

Checkpoint: one credential, github-main-branch, with issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, your subject, and audience api://AzureADTokenExchange.

Task 7 · (Optional) Sign in from GitHub Actions without a secret

Do this if GITHUB_REPO is a real repository of yours.

1. Print the values the workflow needs:
  echo "AZURE_CLIENT_ID=$APP_ID"; echo "AZURE_TENANT_ID=$TENANT_ID"
  echo "AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID=$SUB_ID"; echo "AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP=$RG"

2. In GitHub, open the repository's Settings › Secrets and variables › Actions. Add three repository secrets (AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID) and, on the Variables tab, one repository variable (AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP). The IDs aren't secrets; storing them as secrets just keeps them out of logs.
3. On the main branch, create .github/workflows/azure-oidc.yml with the contents of github-workflow-example.yml. Note permissions: id-token: write and the azure/login@v3 step with only three IDs — no client-secret.
4. The commit to main starts the workflow (or use Actions › Azure OIDC sign-in (Lab 22) › Run workflow on main). The sign-in step succeeds, and the next step lists id-nusa-reports and your storage account.
5. Now create a branch called feature/test and run the workflow there. The sign-in fails with AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject … — the subject ends in refs/heads/feature/test, and nothing trusts it. That refusal is the security boundary working.

Checkpoint: a green run on main and a red sign-in on feature/test. If main fails with AADSTS700213 too, copy the subject from the error message (it shows which format your repository uses) and fix GITHUB_REPO in Task 6.

Task 8 · (Read-only tour) Conditional Access and PIM

Conditional Access needs Microsoft Entra ID P1, and Privileged Identity Management and the full access-review feature set need Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance. Microsoft's Entra product pages offer free trials; read the current trial terms first, and remember that when a trial ends, eligible PIM assignments are removed. Without these licences you can still open the pages and read along; you just can't create policies or eligible assignments. Nothing in this task is checked by verify.sh.

Conditional Access — Microsoft Entra admin center › Entra ID › Conditional Access › Policies › New policy:

1. Name: Contractors · Azure management · require MFA.
2. Users: include a contractors group; exclude your emergency-access accounts.
3. Target resources: the cloud app that represents Azure management (search for Azure in the picker).
4. Grant: Grant access › Require multifactor authentication. Session: Sign-in frequency 8 hours.
5. Enable policy: Report-only › Create. Then open Sign-in logs and a sign-in's Report-only tab, and try the What If tool on the policy list, to see what the policy would have done.

Privileged Identity Management — Microsoft Entra admin center › ID Governance › Privileged Identity Management › Azure resources, then select your subscription and rg-lunch22-<suffix>:

1. Settings › Owner › Edit: set Activation maximum duration (1–24 hours), require MFA and a justification on activation, and require approval with at least two approvers.
2. Assignments › Add assignments: role Owner, a member, assignment type Eligible, with an end date.
3. As that member, open My roles › Azure resources and Activate — then watch the assignment become active and expire.

Access reviews — ID Governance › Access reviews › New access review: review the members of a contractors group every quarter, let the group owners decide, and apply results automatically.

Checkpoint: you can explain why every Conditional Access policy starts in report-only with emergency accounts excluded, and what changes when a role is eligible instead of active.

Break it and fix it

Scope creep in a custom role. Dewi says the operator role is "too fiddly" and asks you to "just add Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/* so it always works". Do it:

jq '.Actions += ["Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*"]' my-vm-operator-role.json > my-vm-operator-role-broken.json
az role definition update --role-definition @my-vm-operator-role-broken.json --output none
bash verify.sh

Symptom: after a minute, verify.sh fails Grants no wildcard, write or delete actions. The wildcard quietly added write and delete — the operator could now resize or delete the storefront VM — plus every VM operation Microsoft adds in the future.

Hint: how to fix it

Put the original definition back. az role definition update finds the role by the name in the file and replaces its permissions:

az role definition update --role-definition @my-vm-operator-role.json --output none
az role definition list --name "$ROLE_NAME" --scope "$RG_ID" --query "[0].permissions[0].actions" --output tsv

Lesson: list operations explicitly. If an operator really needs more, add the one action they need — not a wildcard.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

In a safe order, this removes the custom role's assignments and then the role (a custom role can't be deleted while it's assigned), the app registration with its service principal and federated credential (and purges it from Deleted applications), the managed identity and its role assignment, the operators group, the resource group rg-lunch22-<suffix> with the storage account, and the generated my-*.json files. Deletion of the resource group continues in the background for a few minutes. If you did Task 7, also delete the workflow file, secrets and variable from your GitHub repository.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
RoleDefinitionDoesNotExist, or Role 'Nusantara VM Operator …' doesn't exist | The new custom role hasn't replicated yet, or you looked it up at the wrong scope | Wait a minute; look it up with --scope "$RG_ID"; assign it by ROLE_GUID
An error that a role with the same name already exists | You created the role in an earlier attempt | Skip the create command and carry on from the lookup, or use az role definition update
There are existing role assignments referencing role (code: RoleDefinitionHasAssignments) | You tried to delete the custom role while it was still assigned | Remove its assignments first — cleanup.sh does it in that order
MissingSubscriptionRegistration mentioning Microsoft.ManagedIdentity | The resource provider isn't registered in a new subscription | az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ManagedIdentity --wait, then retry
The storage account named stnusareports… is already taken. | Storage names are global and someone has it | Use another name, for example ST_NAME="stnusarpt${SUFFIX}"; verify.sh accepts any storage account in the group
Insufficient privileges to complete the operation. creating the group or app | You can't create directory objects in this tenant | Use the tenant of your personal free account
PrincipalNotFound … does not exist in the directory | The new service principal or group hasn't replicated yet | Wait a minute and retry; keep --assignee-principal-type
GitHub: AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject … | The subject doesn't match: wrong branch, an environment: job, or the immutable format | Copy the subject from the error and create a credential with exactly that value
GitHub: an error mentioning ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL or id-token permissions | The workflow lacks permissions: id-token: write | Add the permissions block from the sample file
GitHub: No subscriptions found for … | The service principal has no role yet, or it hasn't applied | Check Task 5's Reader assignment and wait a few minutes

Stretch goals

- Production-grade subject: add a second federated credential with the subject repo:<owner>/<repo>:environment:production, create a GitHub environment called production with a required reviewer, and add environment: production to the job.
- Federation without an app registration: put the trust on the managed identity instead — az identity federated-credential create --name github-main --identity-name id-nusa-reports --resource-group "$RG" --issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --subject "repo:${GITHUB_REPO}:ref:refs/heads/main" --audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange — and use the identity's client ID in the workflow. Remove it again before you clean up.
- Use the identity for real: attach id-nusa-reports to a small compute resource you create in this resource group (for example a container instance), upload a blob as yourself, and read it from that resource after az login --identity --client-id <the identity's client ID> — no key in sight.
- Test the custom role: add a test user to the operators group (Lab 05 shows how to create one), create a cheap VM in the resource group as yourself ( while it runs), and check that the operator can restart it but not delete it.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), in your own tenant and subscription:

1. A resource group rg-lunch22-<suffix> tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=22.
2. A custom role Nusantara VM Operator <suffix> that allows reading, starting, restarting and deallocating virtual machines, with no wildcard, write or delete actions and no data actions, assignable only at that resource group — and assigned to at least one principal there.
3. A user-assigned managed identity id-nusa-reports in the resource group, holding Storage Blob Data Reader on a storage account in the same group, and no other role.
4. An app registration app-nusa-github-deploy-<suffix> with a service principal, no client secrets or certificates, Reader on the resource group, and a federated credential with issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, audience api://AzureADTokenExchange and subject repo:<owner>/<repo>:ref:refs/heads/main.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
